claims.text: The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
The as-built microstructure is homogeneous and single-phase.
The as-manufactured baseline has no significant oxide scale or internal degradation.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by the evolution and eventual failure of a protective oxide scale.
Oxidizing exposure initially forms a continuous alumina- and/or chromia-rich scale on this alloy.
The initially protective oxide scale retards further oxidation.
The oxide scale accumulates growth or mismatch stresses during elevated-temperature exposure.
Accumulated stresses eventually cause the oxide scale to crack or spall.
Loss of scale integrity produces localized degradation and can cause catastrophic mechanical failure.
A reducing H2-containing atmosphere prevents or limits formation of a continuous protective scale.
The absence of a continuous scale under reducing conditions permits early internal oxidation.
Reducing exposure promotes microstructural coarsening, porosity, or other microstructural destabilization beneath the surface.
Internal oxidation and microstructural destabilization reduce mechanical integrity and accelerate catastrophic failure.
Oxidizing-gas specimens will develop thicker and more continuous surface oxide than the starting-state baseline.
Reducing-gas specimens will have less-developed surface scales but more pronounced internal oxidation than oxidizing-gas specimens.
Changing between oxidizing and reducing atmospheres will systematically alter the time to catastrophic failure and the failure mode.
The proposed mechanism applies over approximately 900–1050 °C and exposure durations up to 12 hours or multiple thermal cycles.
Residual stresses from additive manufacturing may contribute significantly to degradation under the proposed exposure conditions.
